column2: Nat Turner was a literate slave preacher in Virginia who, after an eclipse of the sun, led a revolt that gained some 70 recruits and killed 57 white men, women, and children, leaving whites with a haunting uneasiness.

Gabriel Prosser was a slave blacksmith who recruited perhaps a couple hundred slaves to march on Richmond and capture the governor, but a thunderstorm delayed the attack, the plot was betrayed, and the leaders were captured and executed.
Denmark Vesey was the free Black Charleston carpenter whose 1822 conspiracy, treated more fully in Chapter 11, is cited here as another well-organized uprising that was betrayed and crushed.
William Lloyd Garrison was the editor of The Liberator, whose appearance in the same year as Nat Turner's revolt helped push white southerners toward a closed defense of slavery.

John C. Calhoun called slavery a "positive good," agitated the issue in Congress, demanded censorship of abolitionist mail, and insisted on a gag rule to block antislavery petitions in an effort to unite the South behind his leadership.

James Henry Hammond was a South Carolina planter and senator who declared that cotton was king, admitted that masters had "to rely more and more on the power of fear," and exemplified the large planter's world at Silver Bluff.
Mary Chesnut was a plantation mistress who wrote about miscegenation and the sexual relationships between white men and enslaved women that white wives could not prevent.

Harriet Jacobs, in a narrative the book pairs with Mary Chesnut's, described a mistress who would watch a woman whipped until blood trickled from the lash and spit in the cooking pots so slaves could not eat the leftovers.

Susan Dabney Smedes wrote that "the mistress of a plantation was the most complete slave on it," capturing how heavy a plantation mistress's duties could feel even though she did not share the slaves' oppression.

Frederick Law Olmsted was a northern traveler whose accounts the book uses to describe slave labor in the fields and to quote a yeoman's boast that ordinary whites "would all think themselves as good as" planters.

Sam Williams was an enslaved refiner at Buffalo Forge in the Shenandoah Valley who earned extra money, whose wife Nancy ran a dairy, and whose family the book uses to show that slave life was not everywhere the same.
Ferdinand Steel was a white yeoman in Carroll County, Mississippi, who raised only five or six bales of cotton on 170 acres and never made enough profit to consider buying even one slave.
Octave Johnson was a runaway who lived in the Louisiana swamps with about 30 other fugitives, a portrait the book uses to show day-to-day resistance and the dangers of flight.

Col. Daniel Jordan was a low-country rice planter, master of 261 slaves at Laurel Hill near Charleston, whom the book contrasts with cotton men, industrial slaves, runaways, and yeomen to show how many "real Souths" existed.
